At the housewarming in their Pune flat, Rehana had pulled out Devika's old poetry notebook and read a love poem aloud, doing a silly voice. Everyone laughed. Devika walked out of the room.

That was nine days ago. Since then Devika left for work early, came back late, and walked past Rehana in the kitchen as if she were furniture.

The weight of it sat on Rehana's chest every morning. On the tenth day she wrote a note and slid it under Devika's door: "I read your poem to get a laugh. It was cruel and it was your private writing. I'm sorry. There's no excuse. I won't push you to talk. When and if you want to, I'm here."

Devika didn't answer. Rehana badly wanted to knock, to plead. She didn't. She cleaned the kitchen, paid her share of the bills, and waited. On the fifteenth day there was a cup of tea outside her door.

qa.a: Rehana read a love poem from Devika's old poetry notebook, doing a silly voice.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling during the days of silence?
qa.a: Rehana felt guilty and heavy, with the weight of what she had done sitting on her chest every morning.

qa.q: What was wise about Rehana's apology?
qa.a: It named exactly what she did, made no excuses, and left the choice to talk with Devika instead of pressing her.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt at the housewarming?
qa.a: Devika likely felt humiliated and betrayed, having her private writing mocked in front of everyone.

grounding: The story shows a young woman whose friend refuses to speak to her after being hurt, apologising clearly without excuses and giving space.

"Payal, can I talk to you for two minutes?"

"No, Wasim."

"Please. I just want to say sorry properly."

Payal put her bag down on the library table. "You imitated my stammer in front of the whole seminar group. Everyone laughed. You laughed loudest."

"I know. It was cruel. I'm sorry. I don't have an excuse."

"You said sorry on Tuesday too."

"I did. I'm not asking you to forgive me. I just wanted you to hear it without me trying to explain."

She looked at him for a long time. "I'm still angry. I don't want to talk to you for a while."

Wasim's chest felt heavy. He wanted to argue, to say he'd changed. "Okay," he said. "That's your choice."

He went to the other end of the library. In the next seminar, when someone else laughed at a classmate's accent, Wasim said quietly, "Don't."

qa.a: Wasim imitated Payal's stammer.

qa.a: Wasim felt a heavy chest and the urge to argue, carrying the weight of the harm he had done.

Monday. Noor's father drove to the college in Bhopal after the principal called: Noor had been caught submitting a paid-for project. In the car Papa said only one thing. "We expected better from you." Noor stared at the dashboard, crushed. At home she locked her door and thought, they'll never love me the same way again.

Wednesday. Her brother Vijay knocked. "Papa isn't saying he doesn't love you. He's saying the thing you did was wrong. Those are different." Noor thought about that for a long time. The honest part was true: she had cheated. That part she could own.

Saturday. At breakfast, Noor said to her parents, "You're right, I did something wrong. I've asked the professor to let me redo the project on my own, and I'll accept the penalty." Papa put down his tea. "Good," he said. Then, after a moment, "Pass the jam, beta."

qa.q: What did Papa say in the car?
qa.a: Papa said, "We expected better from you."

qa.q: How did Noor feel after Papa's words, and what did she believe?
qa.a: Noor felt crushed and believed her parents would never love her the same way again.

qa.q: What helped Noor move from shame to repair?
qa.a: Vijay helped her see disappointment in an act is different from rejection, so she owned the cheating and shared a plan to redo the project.

Aadhya, you think your parents will never forgive you for failing that semester? Let your Pradeep dada tell you what happened in 1970. I was twenty, studying in Allahabad, and I skipped classes for months to play cards. I lied in every letter home. When the results came, I had failed three subjects.

My father came on the train. He didn't shout. He said, "We expected better from you, Pradeep." That was worse than shouting. I felt like a stone had been put on my chest. I thought I had lost him.

That night I sat on the ghat for hours. Then I understood: he was disappointed in what I did, not finished with who I was.

In the morning I told him the truth about the cards and the lies. I showed him a timetable I'd written, for the re-exams. He read it, folded it into his pocket, and took me to eat kachori.

qa.a: He had failed three subjects.

qa.a: Young Pradeep felt crushed, as if a stone had been put on his chest, and feared he had lost his father's love.

In the small government school outside Nashik where Eshaan had started teaching, the headmaster pinned the district scholarship notice for young teachers on the board. Eshaan read it three times and walked away.

That week he had written a wrong answer on the blackboard in a maths lesson, and a sharp girl in the front row had pointed it out. The children giggled. Eshaan had felt like the floor opened. That night he redid every lesson plan for the month, until the lamp oil ran low.

Bhavna, who taught the fourth standard, found him in the staff room at seven, red-eyed. "You didn't sleep. Over one sum?" He nodded. "And now you won't apply for the scholarship?"

"What if I fail at that too?"

"Then you'll learn something. Like the girl who corrected you."

He laughed, a little. That afternoon, he told the headmaster about the blackboard mistake, and asked for the scholarship form.

The customer's SUV was due back at five, it was already three, and Baljeet had just cross-threaded the oil drain plug. The garage in Ludhiana went quiet. He stood over the car, hands black, face burning. The voice in his head was loud: you're useless, you'll be sent back to the village.

Chaitanya, the head mechanic, came over, looked, and then laughed. "I once put diesel in a petrol car. At your age. The owner chased me down the road." Then, more seriously: "So. What will you do now?"

Baljeet felt his breathing slow. Something in his chest steadied.

"Retap the thread. Fit an oversize plug. Tell the customer honestly."

"Good. Go."

He worked carefully, not fast. At 4:50 the car was ready. He explained the fix to the customer himself. That evening he stayed back to practise threading on an old sump. Grace, he thought, is for getting up, not for being sloppy.

qa.a: It was due back at five.

Tanuja's first front-page story for the Kolkata daily had the wrong name for the school principal. By 9 am the school had called. By ten she was sitting in the editor's cabin, hands cold, sure this was the end.

Tarun, the news editor, read the complaint and put it down. "When I was your age I once reported a man dead who was very much alive. He came to the office to complain in person." He smiled a little. "I made worse mistakes than this. Now, what will you do?"

Something in Tanuja loosened. Not relief exactly. Firm ground.

"Call the principal and apologise. Write the correction for tomorrow. And make a checklist for names."

"Then do it."

She did all three before lunch. The checklist went on her desk, and she used it every night after that, even on small stories.

In the Hyderabad flat, the argument began over something small. Vidya had insisted, at dinner with friends, that the old fort was built by the Mughals. Ishita, who studied history, said gently that it was the Qutb Shahi kings. Vidya laughed and said, "Trust me." When Ishita showed the page on her phone, Vidya said the website was wrong.

Later, washing dishes, Vidya's face still burned. Admitting it felt like admitting she was stupid, that she didn't belong at a table of clever people. So she had doubled down, and everyone had gone quiet.

She noticed Ishita hadn't spoken to her since.

Vidya dried her hands. She knocked on Ishita's door. "I was wrong about the fort. And I was rude to you when you were right. I'm sorry."

Ishita looked surprised, then smiled. "Thanks. That actually makes me trust you more." Vidya felt oddly lighter, not smaller.

Friday night

The results came at noon. I didn't clear the prelims, second year in a row. I'm Bhupen. I sat in the cyber café staring at my roll number not being there, and I wanted to disappear.

Santosh called. I nearly didn't pick up. I didn't want his pity, didn't feel I deserved anyone being nice to me. He didn't ask about marks. He said, "Come, let's eat. The dhaba near the bridge. I'm leaving now."

We ate rotis and dal fry and he talked about his cousin's wedding, the cows that walked into the tent. I laughed. Actually laughed. He never once said "next year" or "you should have".

Walking back, I told him I didn't know what to do next. He said, "Not tonight. Tonight you ate." I felt held.

Tomorrow I'll look at the paper again, and think about what comes next. Tonight, I ate.

Results day at the coaching centre in Patna, and the hall was packed, hot, noisy. The bank exam list went up on the board. Parveen's roll number wasn't there. Ramesh's was. So were two others from her batch who, she thought bitterly, had barely studied.

A hard knot twisted in her stomach. Part of her wanted to say something sharp, to walk out without a word to Ramesh.

She noticed the feeling. Jealous, she told herself. Okay. That's what this is.

Then she pushed through the crowd. "Ramesh. Congratulations. Really." He looked surprised, and pleased.

"Can I ask you something? What did you do differently this time?"

"Mock tests every Sunday," he said. "And I stopped reading new books in the last month. Only revision." He hesitated. "Want to join our Sunday group?"

She said yes. The knot didn't vanish. But it loosened.

Pallavi and Nitin, married two years. During the session, whenever Nitin spoke, Pallavi rolled her eyes or gave a short laugh. When he described how he likes to plan holidays, she said, "Of course, because God forbid anything is spontaneous." Nitin's shoulders dropped and he stopped talking.

Homework: one direct request each, daily.

- Madhuri

Bhupen came alone this week. He spoke quietly, looking at his hands. At home, his wife, Priti, sneers when he talks about his work at the cooperative bank. "Oh, the big banker speaks." In front of her friends she corrects his English. He said, "I've started not talking at dinner. I feel small in my own house. I feel unsafe to say anything."

We practised a calm sentence together: "When you mock how I speak, I feel small. I need you to speak to me with respect." He said it three times before his voice stopped shaking.

- Usha

Sunday, late

Ojas did it again at his parents' anniversary lunch. When I said I'm thinking of doing a pottery course, he laughed and said to his cousins, "Omkar and his little hobbies. Next it'll be knitting." Everyone laughed. I laughed too, and then couldn't eat.

passage:
I'm Hansa, and the worst fights in my marriage used to go like this. Mohit would raise his voice, about money, about his mother's visits, and I'd go silent. Completely. I'd walk into the bedroom and lock the door and not speak for two days. He'd get louder. I'd get colder.

Last month it started again. He was shouting that I never make time for his family. My heart was hammering and I wanted to run.

But I remembered what my friend Gopika told me: say you need a break, and say when you'll come back.

So I said, "I hear that you feel your family's left out. I'm feeling flooded. I need forty-five minutes. I'll come back to the balcony at nine."

He stopped mid-sentence. At nine I came back. We talked for an hour, quietly. It wasn't solved. But nobody locked a door.

qa.a: Hansa named the complaint under the shouting, asked for forty-five minutes and came back at nine, instead of stonewalling for two days.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt when Hansa used to lock the door for two days?
qa.a: Mohit likely felt shut out and more upset, which is why he got louder.
